drapeaux.note: Quoted from the Swiss Parliament blog, published in French (and German); no English version of the page found, so translated from the French.

titre: Switzerland's First Labor Law Protects Mothers by Taking Away a Choice
accroche: In 1877, Switzerland's first federal labor law bans women factory workers from working for six weeks after giving birth.
contenu_vulgarise:
Bern, October 21, 1877. In a referendum, the Swiss people accept, by 181,204 votes to 170,857, the federal law on work in factories, passed seven months earlier by the National Council, on March 23, by 90 votes to 15. The law takes effect on January 1, 1878. For the first time, the Confederation itself legislates on working conditions: until then, worker protection had remained a cantonal matter, and only nine cantons had regulated it before 1877, three of them for women workers alone.

## Eleven Hours, Fourteen Years, Six Weeks

The text sets the normal working day at eleven hours, ten on Saturdays, regulates night and Sunday work, and bans the employment of children under fourteen. It establishes the employer's civil liability in the event of an accident and creates a corps of federal inspectors tasked with checking, factory by factory, that these rules are respected, a novelty at a time when the workshop was still the boss's private domain. Finally, the law contains one provision specific to women: it forbids them to work during the six weeks following childbirth.

## A Protection That Also Deprives

This last rule had drawn opposition, even before its adoption, from an unexpected camp. In 1875, the workers of the Robert & Cie ébauches factory (a maker of unfinished watch movements) in Fontainemelon, in the canton of Neuchâtel, sent a petition to the Federal Assembly. They feared being put at a disadvantage against workers in other countries, free to work eighteen hours a day, but they also added that preventing women from deciding for themselves when to go back to work after childbirth was, in their view, an affront to them. The law protects women workers' health by taking away, for six weeks, their ability to choose.

It is the same gesture found in much of the earliest social legislation: protection and tutelage advance together, because the nineteenth-century law that removes a person from a danger rarely does so by asking for their opinion. The debate raised by Neuchâtel watchmaking workers in 1875, whether removing someone from a risk in the name of their health also deprives them of a decision that belongs to them, predates by a century the contemporary discussions of consent in labor law.

repere.texte: On October 21, 1877, the law is accepted by the Swiss people by 181,204 votes to 170,857, thanks to the support of the German-speaking cantons. [...] It limits the standard working day to eleven hours, regulates night and Sunday work, and prohibits the hiring of children under 14. The law also prevents women from being employed during the six weeks following childbirth.
repere.source: Swiss Parliamentary Services, “The Factory Act, the first intervention of the State in freedom of contract,” October 19, 2022

carte.punch: Switzerland's 1877 federal law protects mothers by taking away their choice
carte.idee: In 1877, Switzerland's first federal labor law bans women from working for six weeks after giving birth. In 1875, workers in Neuchâtel had written to the Federal Assembly that preventing women from deciding for themselves when to return to work was an affront.

quiz.question: Why did the provision of the 1877 Swiss law banning women from working during the six weeks after childbirth draw opposition from workers even before its adoption?
choix: Because the ban applied only to married women, leaving other women workers unprotected
Because the law provided no penalty for employers who failed to comply with it
Because doctors of the time considered six weeks too short and recommended a longer leave
Because some workers saw it as an infringement on women's freedom to decide for themselves when to return to work
quiz.explication: In 1875, the workers of the Robert & Cie factory in Fontainemelon sent a petition to the Federal Assembly: preventing women from choosing for themselves when to return to work after childbirth was, in their view, an affront to them, not a mere protection.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Apart from Saturday, how long is the normal working day set by the 1877 law?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law sets the normal day at eleven hours, and only ten on Saturday; eight and twelve hours appear nowhere in the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before the 1877 federal law, how many Swiss cantons already regulated worker protection?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Only nine cantons had legislated on worker protection before 1877, three of them only for women workers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What institutional novelty does the 1877 law create to check its application in factories?
choix: A fine paid directly to injured workers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law establishes a corps of federal inspectors tasked with checking each factory, a novelty when the workshop was still a private domain.
